newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan issues mild warning on stock manipulation.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan issues mild warning on stock manipulation.

text.p: Taiwan regulators have issued a mild warning on stock manipulation to local mutual funds after soaring turnover cast a harsh light on what analysts called questionable investment practices of some fund managers.
The Securities and Exchange Commission said its officials held a seminar with chief executives of 20 securities investment trust firms and warned them not to manipulate stocks.

"We...urged them not to get involved in listed firms' management and not to cooperate with major market players to jointly manipulate stock prices," a commission official, referring to the Tuesday seminar, told Reuters.
"But please don't interpret this as a move to cool down the market," the commission official added.

Analysts said the agency used quiet moral persuasion rather than a more public rebuke because it wanted to warn mutual funds about manipulation without putting a damper on the market, which has turned bullish again after a late March correction.
"The SEC hopes to see a bullish stock market, but it also is afraid that the market might be getting too speculative," said HSBC James Capel senior analyst Alex Chen.

The official said the commission issued a warning last week to four of the 20 securities trust firms, rapping them for "inappropriate actions" in the management of closed-end funds in a bid to prevent them from being converted into open-end funds.
"We told them such moves aren't allowed," he said. "We want them to make investments according to their research results."

The commission convened the closed-door seminar on Tuesday, just hours after turnover in the stock market soared to a record T$238.9 billion (US$8.69 billion) -- putting Taiwan into the ranks of the world's top markets in terms of turnover.
Analysts said much of the staggering turnover reflected strategic trades between managers of closed-end mutual funds in a quest to stave off their conversion into open-end funds.

A closed end fund does not typically issue new shares nor redeem old ones. Its shares are bought and sold like stock on the stock exchange and over the counter. In an open-end fund share capital can be increased.
"Such trading of course is manipulation, but the question is it's very hard to get the evidence," said one senior brokerage manager who declined to be named in such a sensitive issue.
"Some fund firms had jointly sold certain shares that their internal research reports recommended as 'buys'," he said.

According to exchange rules, investors can demand that any closed-end fund whose market price shows a 20 percent discount to the net asset value of its component stocks for more than 20 straight sessions be converted into an open-end fund.

Brokers said big investors, including foreign funds, had been actively selling shares closed-end funds that were nearing conversion, assuming that this would ensure the 20 percent discount and force the closed-end funds to convert -- giving them a crack at quick conversion profits of up to 20 percent.

Brokers said the closed-end funds fought back by buying shares from each other to ensure the 20 percent discount was not sustained, thereby reducing the likelihood that the funds would be obliged by shareholders to convert.
Some of the closed-end funds' major investors -- many of them are Taiwan conglomerates -- also tried to buy up fund shares to prevent them from being converted.
Brokers said Tuesday's record turnover should be seen as normal from now on.

Nikko Securities research head Leonard Hsueh said the previous record of T$216 billion (US$7.85 billion) set in March 16, 1990, was equivalent to T$395 billion (US$14.3 billion) today if the change in money supply is considered.
Local institutional investors, including mutual funds and securities brokerages, accounted for 8.6 percent of the market's total value in 1996, according to the securities commission.

Foreign funds took 2.1 percent, while individual investors represented 89.3 percent. This compared to a ratio of more than 50 percent by institutional investors in most industrialised countries, analysts said.
